item.title: Anti-Environmentalism and the Future of Green Growth
item.content:encoded:
Anastasios Xepapadeas, Athens University of Economics and Business

Simone Marsiglio, University of Pisa

Luca Gori, University of Pisa

The special issue examines anti-environmentalism—opposition to environmental regulation, renewable energy expansion, and climate mitigation efforts—and its implications for achieving green growth and sustainable development. It addresses how public attitudes, political polarization, and institutional factors shape the feasibility and design of environmental policies in the context of escalating climate risks and planetary boundaries.

The collection seeks research across environmental economics, macroeconomics, political economy, and behavioral economics that explores the causes, dynamics, and consequences of anti-environmental movements for sustainable economic transitions. It welcomes diverse methodological approaches, with particular emphasis on studies that clarify the complex relationships between anti-environmentalism, economic incentives, and policy effectiveness in facilitating low-carbon development.

Appel publié par Environmental and Resource Economics. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Economic, social and political determinants of anti-environmental attitudes and behavior
  • The impact of populism, misinformation, and lobbying on climate and environmental policy outcomes
  • Public perception and resistance to carbon taxation, green industrial policies, and regulation
  • Distributional and equity aspects of green growth as sources of policy backlash
  • The role of institutions and governance in shaping environmental resistance
  • International and comparative analyses of anti-environmental movements and climate cooperation
  • Behavioral and cultural dimensions of environmental skepticism and pro-growth narratives
  • Policy strategies for overcoming anti-environmentalist sentiment and fostering green, just and inclusive transitions
  • Economic growth under increasing climate-related extreme event risk, and the costs of climate skepticism

Timeline

  • March 31, 2027: Submission deadline

item.title: Behavioural Environmental Economics & Policy (BEEP): trends and reflections
item.content:encoded:
Sanchayan Banerjee, King's College London

Lory Barile, University of Warwick

This special issue focuses on Behavioural Environmental Economics & Policy (BEEP), which examines how departures from rational choice assumptions—such as bounded rationality and bounded willpower—affect environmental decision-making and policy effectiveness. The issue seeks to consolidate evidence on how behavioural insights can improve the design and evaluation of environmental policies to address urgent challenges including climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution.

The special issue welcomes conceptual, empirical, and policy-oriented contributions applying behavioural insights to environmental problems. Submissions may employ various methodologies including experiments, quasi-experimental designs, and literature reviews. The issue particularly values work that identifies both market and behavioural failures, designs and tests policies combining traditional instruments with behavioural tools, and evaluates their effectiveness and welfare impacts.

This is an invitation-only special issue in Environmental and Resource Economics.

Appel publié par Environmental and Resource Economics. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Interactions between market failures and behavioural failures in environmental settings
  • Policy design that combines prices/standards with behavioural tools (defaults, salience/framing, simplification, commitment)
  • Welfare analysis (including psychological costs), ethics, and paternalism in environmental policy
  • Empirical identification of behavioural mechanisms; field/lab/quasi-experimental evidence
  • Heterogeneity, equity, and distributional consequences of behavioural environmental policies
  • Replication, meta-analysis, and open-science practices in this domain
  • Choice architecture and environmental outcomes
  • Interactions between behavioural instruments and prices/regulation
  • Climate cognition and communication
  • Evaluation and methods

Timeline

  • November 30, 2026: Submission deadline

item.title: Valuing health and longevity: Advances and innovations
item.content:encoded:
Lisa A. Robinson, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health

Olof Bystrom, OECD

Ståle Navrud, Norwegian University of Life Sciences

Mortality risks are central to environmental policy benefit assessments, yet the value per statistical life literature has notable gaps regarding population attributes, risk characteristics, and how to synthesize findings across contexts. Nonfatal health impacts receive limited attention despite their substantial contribution to policy benefits, and their valuation relies heavily on proxy measures like averted costs rather than willingness-to-pay estimates.

This special issue seeks recent research addressing these challenges, including improved willingness-to-pay studies for mortality and morbidity effects, better methods for combining and transferring valuation results, and innovative approaches to distributional equity and co-occurring effects in health benefit assessment.

Appel publié par Environmental and Resource Economics. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Value per statistical life (VSL) and mortality risk valuation
  • Population and risk attributes affecting VSL estimates
  • Synthesis and application of VSL estimates
  • Nonfatal risk reductions and morbidity valuation
  • Willingness to pay (WTP) for health risk reductions
  • Cost-benefit analysis for environmental policies
  • Benefit transfer and evidence synthesis across studies
  • Distributional equity in health valuation
  • Co-occurring health effects and combined valuation approaches

Timeline

  • November 30, 2026: Submission deadline

item.title: Wildfires in a Changing Climate: Impacts, Adaptation, and Policy
item.content:encoded:
Sarah Meier, ETH Zurich

Eric Strobl, University of Bern

Robert J. R. Elliott, University of Birmingham

Wildfires are becoming increasingly frequent and intense in many regions due to climate change, land-use shifts, and expanding human settlements in fire-prone areas. Their economic impacts extend far beyond direct suppression costs, affecting labour productivity, supply chains, tourism, housing markets, and public health through smoke exposure. Rising public expenditures on prevention and recovery, combined with evolving policy debates around insurance and risk financing, underscore the need for rigorous economic analysis.

This special issue seeks empirical research that quantifies the welfare consequences of wildfires and smoke, particularly in regions facing emerging risks and in developing economies. The call welcomes interdisciplinary work grounded in environmental and resource economics that evaluates adaptation and management strategies, leveraging new data sources and innovative methodologies including remote sensing and AI-based technologies.

Appel publié par Environmental and Resource Economics. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Labour productivity, sectoral employment shifts, and worker mobility
  • Housing markets, mortgage risk, and migration and other behavioural responses to wildfire risk and exposure
  • Natural capital and ecosystem service valuation, including impacts on biodiversity, recreation, and forest asset pricing
  • Inequality, information access, and distributional impacts of exposure and monitoring technologies
  • Public finance, insurance markets, and the fiscal consequences for local and regional governments
  • Institutions, governance, and risk-sharing arrangements, including coordination across jurisdictions, public-private roles, and firm responses to wildfire risk
  • Prevention, suppression, and adaptation strategies, including land-use planning, prescribed burning, indigenous fire stewardship, and advanced monitoring and management technologies
  • Welfare losses from smoke exposure, including physical and mental health outcomes and associated human capital effects

Timeline

  • January 31, 2027: Submission deadline
